analysis.title: Paul Donovan's daily audio: Shifting expectations
key_insights: Markets responded positively to the US midterm election results. UBS expects policy gridlock to reduce politicians' ability to do further fiscal damage, but it does not fix the unsustainable US fiscal position.
US Vice President Vance blamed Republican midterm losses on the Gulf war. UBS says this, amplified by optimism bias, shifted expectations toward a US retreat and allowed oil prices to fall.

German September factory orders grew in line with expectations, and past data was revised stronger. UBS argues the repeated pattern of weak initial German data followed by upward revisions weakens the narrative about the German economy.

Eurozone producer price inflation is expected to keep rising, as consumer price data did. Producer prices are more exposed to energy prices than consumer prices, which are dominated by labor costs that dilute the effect of the Gulf war.
US preliminary productivity and unit labor cost data are due. Productivity figures are prone to revision, but Fed Chair Warsh places weight on productivity, so the figures matter more.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Past data was revised stronger. UBS says repeated weak initial prints followed by upward revisions undermine the German economic narrative.
Producer prices are more exposed to energy costs than consumer prices, so the Gulf war's energy effects show up here more.

macro_indicators.indicator: US preliminary productivity and unit labor costs
macro_indicators.interpretation: Productivity is a residual and prone to revision. Fed Chair Warsh emphasizes productivity, which raises the data's importance for policy.

risk_factors: The US fiscal position remains unsustainable even with expected gridlock.
Productivity data are subject to large revisions.
Energy price effects from the Gulf war continue to push up producer prices.
geopolitical: Gulf war: US Vice President Vance blamed Republican midterm losses on it, and UBS says expectations of a US retreat allowed oil prices to fall.
The Gulf war's energy price effects are cited as pushing up eurozone producer prices.
